# Loading and Cleaning

First we load our data to remember what they are about:

```{r}
ess_pol <- read.csv('ess_pol.csv', sep = ',')
head(ess_pol)
str(ess_pol)
```

Let us cleanup and save our data

```{r}
# Clean four/two-digit key-codes
for (v in c(77, 88, 99, 6666, 7777, 8888, 9999)) {
  ess_pol <- ess_pol[rowSums(ess_pol == v, na.rm = TRUE) == 0, ]
}
summary(ess_pol)
```

Also, since countries form a categorical variables, we should treat it as a factor:

```{r}
ess_pol$ess_data.cntry <- as.factor(ess_pol$ess_data.cntry)
str(ess_pol)
```

Since we are using this a lot, we should also save the cleansed values:

```{r}
write.csv(ess_pol, 'ess_pol_clean.csv', sep = ',')
```

# A First Theory

One idea, given the variables we have chosen is to look for any effects of the time
people devote on politics news and the time they spend on the internet on a daily basis on their level of other people trust. Also, we should, most probably, take also countries into account or focus, first to a single country.

First, let us quickly look for potential correlations between ppltrst and the rest of our variables:


```{r}
pairs(ess_data.ppltrst ~ ., data = ess_pol)
```
Too much noise! So, first, we might want to study a particular country and then repeat maybe for all.

```{r}
ess_pol_den <- ess_pol[ess_pol$ess_data.cntry == 'DK', ]
str(ess_pol_den)
```
Okay, so, accidentally, we see that all Danish responses have been removed from our data. To test whether this is a general thing or just affects danish submissions
we can create a barplot of our country counts:

```{r}
cntry_tab <- table(ess_pol$ess_data.cntry)
plot(cntry_tab, las = 2)
```

It seems that danish participats were maybe too few and all of them have been excluded. To verify this, we just reload our data on a separate dataframe and plot the same barplot for them:

```{r}
or_data <- read.csv('ess_pol.csv', sep = ',')
or_data$ess_data.cntry <- as.factor(or_data$ess_data.cntry)
plot(table(or_data$ess_data.cntry), las=2)
```

So, thankfully enough, we have not eliminated danish participants, it is just that they were never there!

So, let us pick Italy, instead:

```{r}
ess_pol_it <- ess_pol[ess_pol$ess_data.cntry == 'IT', ]
summary(ess_pol_it)
```

So, now, let us create those correlation plots on the above data:

```{r}
pairs(ess_pol_it$ess_data.ppltrst ~ ess_pol_it$ess_data.netustm + ess_pol_it$ess_data.nwspol, data = ess_pol_it)
```

So, let us also compute the corresponding correlations:

```{r}
cor(ess_pol_it[, c('ess_data.ppltrst', 'ess_data.netustm', 'ess_data.nwspol')])
```

All correlations in this case, appear to bee too weak to be considered, so, we drop the idea of investigating further by using linear regression.

# What If...?

There are too many extreme values in the above, e.g., TV attendance of more than 1000 minutes per day, so we might also consider excluding extreme values:

```{r}
ess_pol_it <- ess_pol_it[ess_pol_it$ess_data.netustm <= 600, ]
ess_pol_it <- ess_pol_it[ess_pol_it$ess_data.nwspol <= 600, ]
```

Now, let us compute correlations again:

```{r}
cor(ess_pol_it[, c('ess_data.ppltrst', 'ess_data.netustm', 'ess_data.nwspol')])
```
Since correlations found are still too weak, we just drop this hypothesis.
